title: Volume 7 · Projects, Timesheets and Billable Work
subtitle: Lessons 1–4: a project that carries its own profit and loss, timesheets that become invoices, and a close that shows the margin
outcomes: Set up a project whose cost and revenue land on the same report
Record billable and non-billable time without inflating the client invoice
Turn approved timesheets into an invoice with the right tax treatment
Report project margin and close the project with evidence

slides.title: Create a project that tracks its own profit
bullets: A project is a cost collector, and its value appears only if every entry names it
Set the expected start and end dates, because they drive the billing schedule
Assign a cost centre if the client reports by department as well as by project
Create the project before the first timesheet, not after the first invoice

rows: Project currency MYR, 150.00 per hour billing rate
Retail Counter - SM for delivery work
Zero hours, zero cost, zero billed

slides.notes: The billing rate on the project is what turns hours into money, so get it agreed in writing before the first timesheet. Twenty hours at one hundred fifty is three thousand of revenue, and the client will compare that against the fixed quote in the contract. A project without a rate produces timesheets that finance has to reprice by hand, which is exactly the work a consultant is hired to remove.

slides.title: What the project must carry before work starts
bullets: Rate, cost centre, dates and customer are the four fields that matter
A project with no customer cannot be invoiced without retyping everything
Cost centre makes the project visible in departmental reporting as well
The percentage complete figure is a management input, not an accounting one
slides.notes: Twenty hours at one hundred fifty is three thousand, and the expected cost will come from timesheets at the internal rate. Writing both numbers down before work starts is what makes the margin conversation possible in week three, when the client asks why the invoice is higher than they remember.

slides.title: Record time so it can be billed and costed
bullets: A timesheet records hours against a project and an activity, and it carries a cost
Mark billable time deliberately, because non-billable hours still cost money
Approve timesheets before invoicing, or the invoice will not be defensible
The internal cost rate is separate from the billing rate and is what finance needs

rows: Employee Aina, project Aeon Big rollout

slides.notes: Eight billable hours at one hundred fifty and two non-billable at the same rate is a trap, because non-billable time must not reach the invoice. Marking it correctly keeps three thousand of revenue intact while still costing eight hundred, which is the honest picture. Teach the difference before the first timesheet, not after the first disputed invoice.

slides.title: Turn approved time into a defensible invoice
bullets: Invoicing from a timesheet carries hours, rate and project onto the invoice automatically
Service tax treatment differs from goods, so check the template before submitting
An invoice without a project loses the margin link that made the project worth creating
Bill monthly, because a single invoice at the end hides cost overruns until it is too late
slides.notes: Twenty hours at one hundred fifty is three thousand of revenue, twenty hours at eighty is one thousand six hundred of cost, and the difference of one thousand four hundred is the margin the project exists to produce. Service tax of eight per cent adds two hundred forty, which is a liability and never revenue. When those three numbers are visible on one screen, the client stops treating projects as a reporting nicety.

slides.title: Close the project with the numbers attached
bullets: Closing means no more time or cost can be posted against the project
Compare final cost with the estimate and write down the reason for the difference
Unbilled timesheets must be invoiced or written off before closing
A closed project is the reference for pricing the next one

rows: Filter timesheets by project and billing status
Signed timesheet and invoice in the file
Variance note in the project sheet

slides.notes: The value of closing properly is the next quotation. A project that ended at one thousand six hundred of cost against an estimate of one thousand two hundred teaches the client to reprice, provided somebody writes it down. Make the variance note part of the close, or the same underestimate will repeat on every engagement and the consultant will be blamed for the system's silence.

slides.title: Project documents and the controls they carry
bullets: Each document adds one dimension: time, cost, revenue or status
The project record is the join between all four, which is why it must be named everywhere
Approval is the control that makes timesheets billable and defensible
Every control has an owner in the client's team, not in the consultant's head
slides.notes: Projects fail in ERPNext for a boring reason: somebody forgets to name the project on a timesheet, and the cost disappears into a departmental expense. The fix is a control, not a report, so agree who checks that every timesheet carries a project and put it in the weekly meeting. When that control is in place, the margin report is trustworthy by default.

slides.title: Reading the project profit and loss
bullets: Revenue comes from invoices that name the project, not from quotations
Cost comes from timesheets and purchase documents that name the project
Unbilled work in progress is a real asset, and it belongs in the month-end pack
A margin of 46 per cent on services is healthy for Malaysian implementation work
slides.notes: Show this page to the client's finance manager and to the engagement manager in the same meeting, because they will each read a different line. Finance wants unbilled time at zero; the engagement manager wants margin above forty per cent. When both are on one page, the project review takes ten minutes instead of an hour.

lab.title: Lab · Run a 20-hour project from setup to margin
steps: Create the Aeon Big rollout project with a 150.00 billing rate and a cost centre
Confirm the expected revenue of 3,000.00 before any work is recorded
Record 20 billable hours and 2 non-billable hours on a timesheet
Submit the timesheet and confirm the project cost of 1,600.00
Create the sales invoice from the timesheet with 8 per cent service tax
Confirm net revenue 3,000.00, tax 240.00 and total 3,240.00
Read project profitability and confirm the 1,400.00 margin
Close the project and confirm new timesheets are refused
lab.done: Done when the project shows 3,000.00 revenue, 1,600.00 cost and 1,400.00 margin, no unbilled time remains, and the project no longer accepts postings.

quiz.question: 20 billable hours at 150.00 with 8 per cent service tax give aninvoice total of what?
quiz.why: Net is 3,000.00 and service tax of 8 per cent adds 240.00, giving 3,240.00, of which the tax is a liability not income.

quiz.question: Where does project cost come from?
options: Timesheets and purchase documents naming the project
quiz.why: Only documents that name the project feed its cost, which is why naming the project on a timesheet is the control that matters.

quiz.question: What is the project margin with 20 hours billed at 150.00 and costed at 80.00 per hour?
quiz.why: Revenue is 3,000.00 and cost is 1,600.00, leaving 1,400.00, which is about 46 per cent of revenue.

quiz.question: What happens to non-billable time on a timesheet?
options: It costs the project but is not billed
quiz.why: Non-billable time still carries internal cost, so it reduces margin without appearing on the invoice.

quiz.question: Why close a project in the system?
options: To prevent further postings and capture the variance
quiz.why: Closing stops new time and cost, and the variance note becomes the reference for pricing the next engagement.

memory.spine: A project is a collector, and it only collects what names it, so every hour and every invoice must carry the project field.

device.label: Every entry names the project
expansion: A project is a cost collector whose profit and loss exists only if postings name it
Four fields before work starts: rate, cost centre, dates and customer
A timesheet records hours against project and activity and carries both a billing and a costing rate
Invoice from the timesheet so hours, rate and project travel together
Closing stops time and cost, and does not reverse revenue already billed

cards.q: Why is a project profit and loss empty?
cards.a: Something was posted without the project field, because the collector only sees postings that name it.

cards.q: Where does project revenue come from?
cards.a: Sales invoices that name the project, not quotations and not orders.

cards.q: What does a timesheet carry besides hours?
cards.a: A billing rate and a costing rate, so one hour is both revenue and cost.
Hours, rate and project land on the invoice without retyping, so the margin stays traceable.

cards.q: What does closing a project do?
cards.a: It stops further time and cost postings, and it does not reverse revenue already billed.

trap.what: Hours are captured on the timesheet but the invoice is raised by hand at a different rate.
trap.why: Revenue and cost no longer share a rate, so project margin is fiction and the timesheet becomes paperwork nobody trusts.

narration: Services work is deceptively simple, and the margin is where consultants get caught. A project is a cost collector: name it on a timesheet, name it on an invoice, and it carries both sides. Twenty hours at one hundred fifty is three thousand of revenue; twenty hours at eighty is one thousand six hundred of cost; the difference is one thousand four hundred, about forty six per cent. Service tax of eight per cent adds two hundred forty and stays a liability. Record non-billable time anyway, because it costs money even though it cannot be invoiced. Then close the project with a variance note, which is the only way the next quote gets better. A project that is never closed teaches nobody anything and quietly repeats its mistakes. Twenty hours, one rate, one invoice, one margin: when a client can state those four numbers from memory, the services practice is under control, and the next quotation is priced on evidence rather than optimism.
